result.summary: After the first day's battle, the Thebans set a watch around the Argive camp while Juno sends Sleep to bind them. Thiodamas leads a night raid that slaughters the sleeping Thebans, while Hopleus and Dymas die trying to recover Tydeus' body. At dawn Menoeceus gives his life to save Thebes, and Capaneus scales the wall and is struck down by Jove's thunderbolt.

scenes.title: Thebans besiege the weary Argives
scenes.summary: Night ends the day's fighting. Creon urges his men to ring the Argive camp with watch-fires.
scenes.stakes: The Thebans risk letting the Argives slip away or recover from their defeat.

scenes.title: Argive women pray; Juno sends Iris
scenes.summary: Argive matrons offer a robe to Juno and beg her to destroy Thebes. Angered, Juno sends Iris to Sleep.
scenes.stakes: Argos faces defeat and the loss of its men.

scenes.title: The cave of Sleep
scenes.summary: Iris finds Sleep in his silent cave and delivers Juno's command. Sleep descends on the Theban watch and silences the plain.

scenes.title: Thiodamas proposes a night raid
scenes.summary: Inspired, Thiodamas tells of Amphiaraus' appearance and calls for a raid. Adrastus picks a chosen band.
scenes.stakes: The Argives risk failing to avenge their dead.

scenes.title: Slaughter of the sleeping Thebans
scenes.summary: The raiders cut down the sleeping Thebans. Actor urges restraint and Thiodamas dedicates the spoils to Phoebus.
scenes.stakes: The raiders risk losing divine favour by overreaching.

scenes.title: Hopleus and Dymas die with their chiefs
scenes.summary: Hopleus and Dymas find Tydeus' and Parthenopaeus' bodies by Diana's light, but Amphion's patrol catches them and both die.
scenes.stakes: Their lives and the burial of their princes.

scenes.title: Argive sortie and panic in Thebes
scenes.summary: The Argives return and attack the walls. Thebes is gripped by panic.

scenes.title: Tiresias' oracle and Menoeceus' resolve
scenes.summary: Tiresias reads the omens and demands the last of the serpent's brood. Virtue, disguised as Manto, inspires Menoeceus to accept death.
scenes.stakes: Thebes needs a sacrifice to win; Menoeceus' life is demanded.

scenes.title: Menoeceus' sacrifice and his mother's grief
scenes.summary: Menoeceus deceives his father, kills himself on the wall, and is honoured. His mother laments.
scenes.stakes: Menoeceus gives his life; his parents lose their son.

scenes.title: Capaneus defies Jove
scenes.summary: Capaneus climbs the wall and challenges the gods. Jove strikes him with a thunderbolt.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable maxim on fate's envy of devoted souls.
Capaneus is struck by Jove's thunderbolt.

analysis.text: Night, sleep and divine intervention drive the action, and Menoeceus' voluntary sacrifice contrasts with Capaneus' impious pride.
Statius draws on Virgil's Nisus and Euryalus episode, and the cave of Sleep follows Ovid's description.

legacy.text: Capaneus' defiance of the gods is a famous type of blasphemy, and Dante places him in Inferno 14.

language_notes.text: Pelasgian is used here for the Argives (Greeks generally); Tyrian means Theban, from the Phoenician origin of Cadmus's Thebes.
Danaan: another name for the Greeks or Argives, from Danaus, an ancestor of the Argive kings.
Mycenae stands for the Argive homeland; the Thebans fear the Argives will slip away to it in the night.
Lerna, a marsh near Argos, stands for Argos. The 'black augur' is Amphiaraus, swallowed by the earth; Tydeus died earlier in the war.
'my brother's more cowardly manhood' refers to Polynices, Creon's nephew-by-marriage... in the text it is a taunt aimed at the Argive-allied exile.
Labdacidae: descendants of Labdacus, an early king of Thebes; here simply the Thebans.
Pelopean means Argive, from Pelops, the legendary ancestor of the Peloponnesian peoples; "fane" is an archaic word for temple.
The "Cadmean harlot" is Semele, Cadmus's daughter, whom Jove loved and who bore Bacchus; Juno hated her and Thebes.
Alcmene bore Hercules to Jove, which enraged Juno. The "twofold" adultery likely refers to Jove's two unions with her and Semele, or his double impersonation.
"Aonians" is a poetic name for the Thebans, from Aonia, part of Boeotia.
Mulciber is a name for Vulcan, the smith-god of fire.
"Thaumantian" names Iris as the daughter of Thaumas in myth.
"Sidonian" here means Theban, since Cadmus came from Phoenician Sidon.
The "night-wandering, persuasive deity" is Sleep personified; he withholds his mists from the Greek camp, so the Greeks stay awake.
Saturnia is Juno, daughter of Saturn. Thiodamas is unsure whether she or Apollo inspired him.
The Idaean mother is Cybele, worshipped on Mount Ida. Her Phrygian priests, in ecstasy, cut themselves and beat pine torches against their chests.
"Widowed helm" means the steering oar left without its helmsman; the new officers succeed to command.
Aonian means Theban, from Aonia, a name for Boeotia, the region around Thebes.
Sons of Inachus means the Argives, after Inachus, the river-god and legendary first king of Argos. The Parnassian wreaths are Apollo's priestly emblems.
Pholoë is a mountain in Arcadia known for horse-breeding. The palm of Elis means victory in the Olympic chariot races.
Aeolus is the keeper of the winds, whom he confines in a cave under a mountain.
Polynides is Thiodamas' name for Amphiaraus' son's? No: it refers to Polynices, whose gift of armour the seer now wears.
"Cohorts" here simply means the Theban troop divisions; "torpor" is a deathlike, sluggish sleep.
"Welter of blood" means a heaving, confused mass of blood in which the bodies lie tangled.
Juno, the goddess hostile to Thebes, aids the Argives; her torch is the moon's light, as the translator's note marks.
"Fordone" is archaic for exhausted, worn out. "Aonian" means Theban, from Aonia, part of Boeotia.
"The winged god" is Sleep, who keeps the Thebans unconscious until death; "Sidonians" is a poetic name for Thebans, from Cadmus's Phoenician origin.
"Inachian" means Argive, from the river Inachus near Argos; the prophet is Thiodamas.
Bootes, the Herdsman constellation, flees before the Great Bear's wagon; this marks the hour before dawn.
"Instancy" means urgent pressure; Thiodamas refers to the strain of Phoebus's inspiration upon him.
"Guerdon" is an archaic word for reward or offering; "Paean" and "Lycian god" are titles of Phoebus Apollo.
Cynthia is Diana, named for Mount Cynthus on Delos, her birthplace. The 'threefold' aspect refers to her as Luna in heaven, Diana on earth and Hecate below.
'Stooped her horns' means the crescent moon inclined toward the earth, and her 'chariot' is the moon's course across the sky.
Bacchus was born when his mother Semele was struck by lightning. Ino fled with Palaemon, her young son, and both leapt into the sea. The Thebans honoured them, so Dymas appeals to Theban piety.
'Pelasgians' here is a poetic name for the Greeks, meaning the Argives besieging Thebes.
Euryalus and Nisus are the devoted Trojan ('Phrygian') friends who die together in Virgil's Aeneid. Statius compares his pairs to them.
"Look for his own" means each man searches the returning ranks for his own friend or kinsman.
"The brand called forth from heaven" is a thunderbolt; those struck or stunned by lightning were thought blasted by Jove.
Sidonian means Phoenician; Thebes was traditionally founded by Cadmus, who came from Phoenicia, so poets call Thebans Sidonian or Tyrian.
Ogygian means Theban, from Ogyges, a legendary early king of the region.
The "son of Tyndareus" is Pollux, the boxer-god and a Spartan hero, who shines as a constellation; Alcidamas was his protégé.
The "feigned swan" is Jove, who took swan form to seduce Leda near the Eurotas; the Laconian maiden is Leda.
Ialmenides means son of Ialmenus; the poet names him by patronymic.
"Reins" are the straps by which riders and drivers control the horses.
The "blind tortoise" is a siege shed or testudo, a covered shelter that protects men undermining a wall.
Agenorean means Theban, after Agenor, Cadmus' father; Malea and Ceraunia are capes feared by sailors.
The 'bargained year' refers to the pact that Eteocles and Polynices would rule Thebes in alternate years; Eteocles refused to yield the throne, and the crowd demands he give way.
'Cadmean' means Theban, after Cadmus, the city's legendary founder.
'Labdacus' was an early king of Thebes and the ancestor of its ruling house, so 'sons of Labdacus' means the Theban royal line.
The 'serpent-brood' are the Thebans sprung from the dragon's teeth Cadmus sowed; the 'latest born' must be the youngest of that line, here Menoeceus.
'Guerdon' is an archaic word for reward.
The simile of the Trinacrian (Sicilian) coast beating back the Libyan sea compares Creon's rigid shock to a shore withstanding the waves.
Clio is the Muse of history, invoked here to explain the youth's motive.
Manto is Tiresias' daughter and a seer, so Virtue's disguise as her gives the message credibility.
Amphitryon's son is Hercules, who served the Lydian queen Omphale and wore women's clothes while she wore his lion skin.
'Danaans' is another name for the Greeks, here the Argive attackers.
"Sire" means father; the translation uses archaic "thee/thy" forms throughout.
The "impious dotard" is the blind seer Tiresias; Creon's father-in-law-style slur aside, he is likened to Oedipus, who blinded himself after learning his crimes.
Tiresias' "own daughter" is Manto, who guides him and helps with his prophecies.
"Inachian" means Argive, from Inachus, the river-god and legendary founder of Argos.
"Pelopean" means Greek or Argive, from Pelops; "Oenides" is Tydeus, son of Oeneus.
Lerna was a marsh near Argos, here standing for the Argive army; Inachus is Argos' river-god.
"Tantalid" means descended from Tantalus; here it refers to the Argive host.
The "snake of Mars" recalls the dragon Cadmus killed; its teeth grew into armed men, the ancestors of the Thebans.
"Dugs" are the teats or udders of an animal.
The Aonian groves mean Mount Helicon in Boeotia, home of the Muses. The poet asks for greater inspiration than usual epic requires.
The Stygian sisters are the Furies, goddesses of vengeance, here imagined as driving Capaneus on.
Menoeceus gave his life to Thebes in sacrifice, answering a prophecy. His blood still stains the tower.
The Aloidae, Otus and Ephialtes, were giants who piled Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa to assault heaven.
Bellona is the Roman goddess of war. The Balearic slingers were famed for their skill with slings.
Amphion's lyre was said to move stones into place to build the walls of Thebes, hence the 'unwarlike song'.
Liber is Bacchus, son of Jove and Semele. His 'cradle of fire' recalls Semele's death by Jove's lightning while he was unborn.
Alcides is Hercules, born at Thebes. Capaneus mocks both Theban-born gods as idle.
Phlegra is where the Giants fought the gods and were defeated; Jove cites it as warning against such attacks.
Iapetus was a Titan imprisoned in the underworld; Inarime and Aetna were volcanic isles said to lie over fallen giants.

context_notes.text: Phoebus is the sun god; Jove here orders night to fall and end the day's slaughter.
Creon, the Theban king, speaks as regent after the brothers' conflict; he rallies the exhausted Thebans.
Hippomedon was an Argive champion killed in the fighting; Ismenos is the Theban river, which received his body and armor.
Juno was patron goddess of marriage, so the robe had to be woven by faithful wives, not the childless or separated.
Iris is Juno's messenger and the goddess of the rainbow, which is her "long arc" across the sky.
Sleep's cave lies at the edge of the world in the far west, a traditional setting for the realm of sleep and dreams.
Adrastus is king of Argos and leader of the Greek army besieging Thebes. Many of his chiefs have died.
Amphiaraus, the Argive seer, was swallowed alive by the earth with his chariot. Thiodamas became Apollo's priest in his place.
Capaneus is a proud, violent warrior who despises the gods and scorns stealth.
Thiodamas is the Argive seer who leads this night raid with Actor against the sleeping Theban camp.
The son of Hercules here is Thiodamas's companion among the raiders, alongside Actor; each leads his own band.
Phoebus is Apollo, god of prophecy. Thiodamas serves as his priest, and the tripods are the prophetic seats of his oracles.
Hopleus served Tydeus of Calydon in Aetolia, and Dymas served Parthenopaeus of Arcadia. Both chiefs have died in the night fighting.
Amphion is a Theban officer sent to scout the night and the Argive camp, not the mythical founder of Thebes.
Numidia, in North Africa, was famous for lions and hunters, which makes it a natural setting for the lioness comparison.
Capaneus is the arrogant Argive warrior who scorns the gods, and he is eager for open fighting.
The augur is Amphiaraus, the Argive seer, who foresees the disaster of the expedition and so follows reluctantly.
Mavors is an old Latin name for Mars, the god of war.
Tyrians here means Thebans, whose founder Cadmus came from Tyre.
Tiresias is the blind Theban prophet; his daughter Manto, here called Piety, usually describes the sacrificial signs to him.
Mars was the war god, and the Theban dragon killed by Cadmus was sacred to him, so the oracle demands atonement for it.
The Sphinx on a helmet crest recalls Thebes' old monster and marks Menoeceus' warrior status.
The king is Creon, Menoeceus' father. Tiresias had said Thebes could be saved only if Menoeceus died.
Haemon is Menoeceus' brother, Creon's other son. Menoeceus invents his wound to get away from his father.
Jocasta is Oedipus' mother and wife, and Creon's sister. Her sons Eteocles and Polynices are fighting over the throne.
Capaneus, one of the Seven against Thebes, is known for scorning the gods, and here scales the walls with a ladder-like pathway.
Tritonia is Minerva, a goddess who favoured the Argives. Juno, Jove's wife, also supports Argos.
Semele, Bacchus's mother, was a Theban princess destroyed when she saw Jove in his lightning. Capaneus taunts him with it.

literary_notes.text: Night 'overwhelms' Phoebus, treating day and night as combatants and obedient agents of Jove.
The bloodied plain becomes a 'sea of blood', conveying the scale of the carnage.
The gates, too narrow for the eager rush to battle, are too wide for the thinned returning ranks.
Leaderless Argive bands are likened to ships without helmsmen, left to Chance and storms, conveying their helplessness.
The besiegers are compared to starving wolves around sheepfolds, suggesting predatory hunger and frustrated ferocity.
Quiet, Forgetfulness and Sloth stand as guards, turning abstract states into doorkeepers of Sleep's dwelling.
Silent torrents, reclining sheep and withering buds build a dense picture of stillness, so that even nature seems to sleep.
Death lying hidden with Sleep hints at the killing the sleeping Thebans will soon suffer.
The dreams, true mixed with false, are called the brood of Night, representing the uncertainty of sleeping visions.
Even horses and fires yield to the silence, stressing how total and unnatural Sleep's power is.
Thiodamas' frenzy is compared to a self-wounding priest of Cybele, conveying his possession by the god and making it vivid.
The leaderless ship compares to the Greek army and its untried new chiefs, showing the army's unease without Amphiaraus.
The repeated "himself" and exclamation convey Thiodamas' awe and make his vision sound urgent and certain.
Adrastus choosing among eager youths is likened to a horse-breeder judging his colts, showing his pride and appraising eye.
Adrastus' restraint of the eager warriors is likened to Aeolus blocking the winds in their cave.
The satiated tigress among slain bullocks compares Thiodamas's weary, bloodstained state and thwarted appetite for killing with a predator that has gorged.
The singer spends his last night in music and revelry, unaware that death is near; the lyre becomes his pillow and then the sword's target.
Wine and blood mingling on the tables unites feasting and slaughter in one grim picture.
The narrator suggests that Calpetus's dream warned of Thiodamas and Thebes's ruin, a warning he cannot heed as he dies.
Diana's sudden light is compared to a lightning flash by Jupiter that parts the clouds and reveals the stars, which shows the plain abruptly.
Fate is given envy as a human feeling, and the general maxim prepares the reader for the coming disaster.
Hopleus dies happy in the belief that he still holds Tydeus, although the corpse has been lost, so the sorrow is deepened.
Dymas guarding the body is compared to a lioness over her cubs, fierce but held back by love, which conveys his divided state.
The poet turns to address the dead men directly and promises them lasting fame in his verse.
Eager soldiers on the rampart are compared to nestlings leaning from the nest to meet their mother, giving the scene a tender, protective tone.
The narrator addresses the dying Alcidamas directly, increasing pathos and giving his death a personal tone.
The straining men at the gates are compared to groaning bullocks ploughing, turning war into heavy labour.
Storm clouds that hang over the mountains and then swoop on ships portray the sudden Theban missiles that overwhelm the Argives.
Grief, Fury, Panic and Rout are shown as active demons tearing the city, which makes the terror seem supernatural.
Women arming their men is compared to bees stirred up by a plunderer, ending in a pitiful return to their ruined hive.
The shore resisting the sea mirrors Creon's stunned stillness as grief strikes.
Virtue appears as a goddess who sits beside Jove's throne and chooses to live among worthy men.
The deity's change of appearance lets the divine intervention appear natural and deceives Menoeceus for his own good.
The lightning-struck cypress drinking in flame conveys how swiftly and totally Menoeceus is seized by the desire to die.
The broken syntax, with speech cut short, enacts the shared silence and pain of father and son meeting.
Woe is a "dark cloud" that settles over the father's mind, showing his confusion.
The repeated "now… now" and "he it is" convey Capaneus' relentless, overwhelming violence.
Menoeceus looks as though he had come down from heaven, marking him as already sacred.
The soul disdains its body and grieves at being held fast, so death becomes a release.
The grieving mother's stillness is compared to a tigress robbed of her cubs, whose fury drains into numb desolation.
The poet announces a rise in epic intensity, framing Capaneus's assault on heaven as the poem's grandest moment.
Capaneus is compared to a river wearing down an old bridge, conveying his relentless, unstoppable pressure on the walls.
Bacchus, the god's own son, begs for the thunderbolt that once killed his mother, a bitter reversal.
Jove's calm contrasts with the quarrelling gods, marking his supreme authority.
Capaneus welcomes the lightning as fire for his torch, unaware it will destroy him.
Capaneus keeps standing as he dies, and might merit a second bolt, exaggerating his defiance.
